content: Desiccation refers to a state of extreme dryness or the process of removing moisture to achieve such a state. A desiccant is a hygroscopic material that facilitates or maintains this dryness within its immediate environment, typically in a moderately well-sealed container. In scientific applications, a desiccator is a robust container, often made of glass or plastic, used in practical chemistry to dry or preserve small quantities of materials. The material to be dried is placed on a shelf inside the desiccator, while a drying agent, such as dry silica gel or anhydrous sodium hydroxide, is positioned below the shelf. Many desiccators include a humidity indicator to monitor moisture levels, which changes color to reflect the humidity status. These indicators often use cobalt chloride (CoCl₂) as the active chemical. Anhydrous cobalt chloride appears blue, but when it binds with two water molecules (forming CoCl₂·2H₂O), it turns purple. Further hydration leads to the formation of the pink hexaaquacobalt(II) chloride complex. In biological and ecological contexts, desiccation describes the drying out of living organisms. This can occur when aquatic animals are removed from water or when plants are exposed to intense sunlight or drought conditions. Ecologists often study the vulnerability of various organisms to desiccation as part of their research. In the field of broadcast engineering, desiccators are employed to pressurize the feedline of high-power transmitters. These feedlines, which transmit significant electrical power from the transmitter to the antenna, require a high-quality dielectric material. Air is commonly used as the dielectric because it is lightweight and does not add excessive load to the radio tower. However, moisture can condense within these lines, so desiccated air or nitrogen gas is introduced to prevent this. The pressurization also helps to block water or dampness from entering the feedline at any point along its length.
